findings.claim: The Augustus of Prima Porta breastplate depicts Actium.
findings.truth: The breastplate depicts a Parthian returning Roman standards, not Actium. A dolphin beneath Cupid may allude to Actium.
findings.evidence: Augustus of Prima Porta, Wikipedia, ‘Breastplate relief’: the central scene is the return of standards by Parthia; its Actium reference is the dolphin beneath Cupid.

findings.claim: Trajan’s Column and the Arch of Trajan at Benevento both record the two Dacian campaigns in detail.
findings.truth: Trajan’s Column records both campaigns in detail. The Benevento arch commemorates Trajan’s Dacian triumph but its reliefs also show other imperial and civic activities.
findings.evidence: OCR J199, War and Warfare prescribed sources; Arch of Trajan (Benevento), Wikipedia, description: its frieze shows Trajan’s Dacian triumph, while its panels depict varied imperial activities.

findings.claim: Both Trajan’s Column and the Arch of Trajan at Benevento record the two Dacian campaigns.
findings.truth: Trajan’s Column records both campaigns. The Benevento arch commemorates the Dacian victory alongside other parts of Trajan’s rule.
findings.evidence: Arch of Trajan (Benevento), Wikipedia, description; OCR J199, War and Warfare prescribed sources.

findings.claim: The pilum’s iron shank was deliberately designed to bend or snap on impact.
findings.truth: Option A: retain the conventional explanation that a bent pilum could disable a shield. Option B: teach that the purpose and mechanism are disputed: sources and modern scholars variously describe bending, breaking, or bending as an unintended effect. Revise the related quiz and flashcards together only after choosing an approach.
findings.evidence: Pilum, Wikipedia, ‘Design’: it records competing interpretations, including purposeful bending, breaking, and M. C. Bishop’s later view that bending is unlikely on impact.
findings.ruling: Conventional account kept; one sentence added noting the scholarly debate. Questions unchanged (mark schemes accept the bending account).

findings.claim: Greek heroic culture, especially Tyrtaeus, is framed chiefly as individual glory, unlike Roman collective duty.
findings.truth: Option A: keep individual honour as one strand, but add Tyrtaeus’s civic and collective emphasis. Option B: reframe the comparison around how both traditions combine personal honour with service to the community. This would require coordinated changes across the lesson, conclusion and questions.
findings.evidence: Tyrtaeus, Wikipedia, ‘Poetry’ and ‘Military ideology’: fragment 10 praises noble death, while the discussion also identifies patriotic valour, comradeship and collective victory as central interpretive strands.
findings.ruling: One sentence added to the comparison paragraph giving Tyrtaeus's civic strand; takeaway n20 already hedges; questions keep the exam-level contrast.

findings.claim: “Come back with your shield, or on it” is attributed to Spartan mothers.
findings.truth: The quotation is widely repeated, but its exact wording and attribution were not verified against a fetched primary text in this check.
findings.evidence: No fetched primary-text source confirmed this wording and attribution.

summary: Three precise Lesson 3 corrections address two monument claims. Lessons 2 and 4 contain broader interpretive issues requiring editorial decisions; one unverified quotation is noted.
